_link.title: I can explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction

toLevel2.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
toLevel2.answer: By providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
distractors: By increasing the temperature of the reaction mixture
By increasing the concentration of the reactants
By increasing the kinetic energy of the particles

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst increases reaction rate by lowering the:
distractors: enthalpy change
kinetic energy of particles
concentration of reactants

toLevel2.stem: When a catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway, what happens to the proportion of particles that can react?
distractors: It decreases
It stays the same
It drops to zero

toLevel2.stem: In a catalytic converter, what role does the platinum metal play?
toLevel2.answer: It provides a surface that lowers the activation energy for exhaust gas reactions
distractors: It increases the temperature of the exhaust gases
It increases the concentration of exhaust gases
It adds more reactant particles to the exhaust

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst allows more particles to collide with sufficient energy because:
toLevel2.answer: the energy barrier has been lowered
distractors: the particles have been given more energy
the temperature has been raised by the catalyst
the particles have been made lighter

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst increases reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst increases reaction rate by increasing the kinetic energy of the reactant particles.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction {{blank:1}} with a lower {{blank:2}} energy.
distractors: product
kinetic
system
potential

toLevel2.stem: With a catalyst, more particles can collide with {{blank:1}} energy to react, so the reaction proceeds {{blank:2}}.
distractors: insufficient
slower
excess
backwards

toLevel2.stem: In a catalytic converter, {{blank:1}} metal lowers the activation energy for the conversion of exhaust gases to less harmful {{blank:2}}.
distractors: iron
reactants
copper
catalysts

toLevel3.stem: Why does lowering the activation energy increase the rate of reaction?
toLevel3.answer: A greater proportion of particles already have enough energy to exceed the lower barrier
distractors: The particles gain additional kinetic energy from the catalyst itself
The total number of particles in the system increases when Ea is lowered
Lowering Ea changes the orientation of all particles to be correct

toLevel3.stem: What does 'alternative reaction pathway' mean in the context of catalysis?
toLevel3.answer: A different sequence of bond-breaking and bond-forming steps with a lower energy barrier
distractors: A pathway where the reaction produces entirely different products
A pathway where the reaction does not require any energy at all
A pathway where the reactants do not need to collide with each other

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important that a catalyst does not change the kinetic energy of particles?
toLevel3.answer: It shows the catalyst works by changing the reaction pathway, not the particles themselves
distractors: Changing kinetic energy would make the catalyst more effective
Kinetic energy has no connection to whether particles can react
Catalysts do change kinetic energy but this is not measured

toLevel3.stem: How does understanding catalysis help with later topics on biological enzymes?
toLevel3.answer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower Ea for biochemical reactions
distractors: Enzymes have no connection to catalysis or activation energy
Enzymes work by increasing the temperature inside cells
Enzymes work by increasing the concentration of reactants in cells

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst does not change the overall energy change (ΔH) of a reaction. Why not?
toLevel3.answer: The reactants and products are the same; only the pathway between them changes
distractors: The catalyst absorbs all the energy that would otherwise be released
The enthalpy change depends on the activation energy, which is lowered
The catalyst converts all the enthalpy change into kinetic energy

toLevel3.stem: Why do catalysts speed up both the forward and reverse reactions equally?
toLevel3.answer: The alternative pathway lowers the activation energy for both directions
distractors: Catalysts only speed up the forward reaction, not the reverse
Catalysts only work on exothermic reactions in one direction
Catalysts increase the concentration of products only

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway but does not change the overall enthalpy change of the reaction.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst works by changing the reaction {{blank:1}}, not by changing the {{blank:2}} of the particles.
distractors: products
mass
temperature
number

toLevel3.stem: Enzymes are {{blank:1}} catalysts that lower the activation energy of {{blank:2}} reactions in living organisms.
distractors: industrial
combustion
inorganic
nuclear

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst does not change ΔH because the {{blank:1}} and {{blank:2}} are the same — only the pathway changes.
distractors: temperature
pressure
energy
mass

toLevel4.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly on its own but rapidly when manganese dioxide is added. Using the concept of catalysis, explain why.
toLevel4.answer: MnO₂ provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so more particles can react
distractors: MnO₂ increases the temperature of the hydrogen peroxide solution
MnO₂ increases the concentration of hydrogen peroxide particles
MnO₂ provides additional hydrogen peroxide for the reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student draws an energy profile diagram for a catalysed reaction. The catalysed pathway should show:
toLevel4.answer: a lower peak than the uncatalysed pathway, with the same reactant and product levels
distractors: a higher peak than the uncatalysed pathway to show more energy
the same peak height but different reactant and product energy levels
no peak at all because the catalyst eliminates the activation energy

toLevel4.stem: In the Haber process, an iron catalyst is used to produce ammonia. What does the iron catalyst do?
toLevel4.answer: It lowers the activation energy for the reaction between N₂ and H₂
distractors: It increases the temperature inside the reaction vessel
It provides additional nitrogen and hydrogen molecules
It increases the pressure of the gaseous reactants

toLevel4.stem: A student claims that adding more catalyst will make a reaction even faster. Under what condition is this most likely true?
toLevel4.answer: When the catalyst provides more surface area for reactant particles to interact with
distractors: Adding more catalyst always makes every reaction faster without limit
More catalyst lowers the activation energy further beyond its original level
More catalyst increases the kinetic energy of the reactant particles

toLevel4.stem: A catalytic converter in a car converts CO to CO₂ and NO to N₂. Without the catalyst, these reactions would require very high temperatures. Why does the catalyst avoid this need?
toLevel4.answer: It provides a lower-energy pathway so the reactions proceed at exhaust temperatures
distractors: It heats the exhaust gases to extremely high temperatures inside the converter
It increases the concentration of CO and NO in the exhaust stream
It physically separates the CO and NO molecules to prevent side reactions

toLevel4.stem: A student is told that a catalyst does not appear in the overall equation for a reaction. Why not?
toLevel4.answer: The catalyst is regenerated and is not consumed in the overall process
distractors: The catalyst is destroyed during the reaction and cannot be included
The catalyst becomes part of the products and is included on that side
The catalyst is a reactant that is used up during the reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student wants to speed up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide for a science investigation. They have two options: heat the solution or add MnO₂. Which option lowers the activation energy?
toLevel4.answer: Adding MnO₂ — heating increases particle energy but does not lower Ea
distractors: Heating — temperature always lowers the activation energy of reactions
Both options lower the activation energy by the same amount
Neither option lowers the activation energy of the reaction

toLevel4.stem: On an energy profile diagram, the catalysed pathway has a {{blank:1}} peak than the uncatalysed pathway, while the reactant and product levels remain the {{blank:2}}.
distractors: higher
different
identical
reversed

toLevel4.stem: In the Haber process, an {{blank:1}} catalyst lowers the activation energy for combining {{blank:2}} and hydrogen to form ammonia.
distractors: platinum
oxygen
copper
carbon

toLevel4.stem: A catalytic converter allows exhaust gas reactions to occur at lower temperatures because it provides a pathway with lower {{blank:1}} {{blank:2}}.
distractors: kinetic
levels
thermal
output

toLevel5.stem: A catalyst lowers the activation energy but does not change the enthalpy change. How does this appear on an energy profile diagram?
toLevel5.answer: The peak is lower but the energy levels of reactants and products remain unchanged
distractors: The peak is lower and the product energy level also decreases
The peak stays the same but the reactant energy level increases
Both the peak and the enthalpy change decrease by the same amount

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'A catalyst makes a reaction thermodynamically favourable that was previously unfavourable.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — a catalyst affects kinetics (rate) but does not change thermodynamics (ΔH or feasibility)
distractors: Correct — lowering Ea always makes a reaction more thermodynamically favourable
Correct — catalysts change ΔH from positive to negative, making reactions favourable
Incorrect — catalysts make reactions less thermodynamically favourable

toLevel5.stem: A reaction has Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹ uncatalysed and Ea = 40 kJ mol⁻¹ catalysed. On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, how much more area is now beyond the Ea line?
toLevel5.answer: Significantly more — the area to the right of 40 kJ mol⁻¹ is much larger than to the right of 100 kJ mol⁻¹
distractors: Slightly more — the difference between 40 and 100 kJ mol⁻¹ is negligible
The same — the area does not change when a catalyst is added
Less — lowering Ea reduces the area to the right of the line

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'Since a catalyst is not consumed, it lasts forever.' Evaluate this statement.
toLevel5.answer: Not always — catalysts can be poisoned, degraded, or physically worn over time
distractors: Correct — catalysts are indestructible and never need replacement
Incorrect — catalysts are always fully consumed after one reaction cycle
Correct — catalysts cannot be affected by any external conditions

toLevel5.stem: Why is it that a catalyst speeds up a reaction but cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction spontaneous?
toLevel5.answer: A catalyst only changes the rate by lowering Ea; it cannot change whether ΔG is favourable
distractors: A catalyst can make any reaction spontaneous by lowering Ea enough
A catalyst only works on spontaneous reactions, so non-spontaneous ones are unaffected
A catalyst changes ΔG to be negative, making all reactions spontaneous

toLevel5.stem: A student says: 'Catalysts are specific — each catalyst only works for certain reactions.' Why is this specificity important?
toLevel5.answer: It means the right catalyst must be identified for each reaction — a universal catalyst does not exist
distractors: Catalyst specificity is not real — any catalyst works for any reaction
Specificity only applies to enzymes, not to industrial catalysts
Specificity means catalysts only work at one specific temperature

toLevel5.stem: Compare the effects of a catalyst on the forward and reverse reactions. If the forward Ea is lowered by 30 kJ mol⁻¹, what happens to the reverse Ea?
toLevel5.answer: The reverse Ea is also lowered by 30 kJ mol⁻¹ because the same pathway is used
distractors: The reverse Ea increases by 30 kJ mol⁻¹ to compensate for the lower forward Ea
The reverse Ea stays the same — catalysts only affect the forward reaction
The reverse Ea is lowered by twice as much as the forward Ea

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Adding a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium will shift the equilibrium towards the products.' Is this correct?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — a catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium position is unchanged
distractors: Correct — catalysts always favour product formation over reactant formation
Correct — lowering Ea always shifts the equilibrium towards the products
Incorrect — catalysts shift the equilibrium towards the reactants instead

toLevel5.stem: A catalyst affects the {{blank:1}} of a reaction (how fast it proceeds) but does not change the {{blank:2}} (whether it is energetically favourable).
distractors: thermodynamics
kinetics
products

toLevel5.stem: At equilibrium, a catalyst speeds up both the {{blank:1}} and {{blank:2}} reactions equally, so the equilibrium position does not shift.
distractors: fast
slow
